Abstract.

We demonstrate the breakdown of several fundamentals of Lorentzian causality theory in low regularity. Most notably, chronological futures (defined naturally using locally Lipschitz curves) may be non-open, and may differ from the corresponding sets defined via piecewise 𝒞1\mathcal{C}^{1}-curves. By refining the notion of a causal bubble from [CG12], we characterize spacetimes for which such phenomena can occur, and also relate these to the possibility of deforming causal curves of positive length into timelike curves (push-up). The phenomena described here are, in particular, relevant for recent synthetic approaches to low regularity Lorentzian geometry where, in the absence of a differentiable structure, causality has to be based on locally Lipschitz curves.

Key words and phrases: 
Causality theory, low regularity, chronological future, causal bubbles
2010 Mathematics Subject Classification
53C50; 83C75

1. Introduction

Until a decade ago Lorentzian causality theory had mostly been studied under the assumption of a smooth spacetime metric. However, with the analytic viewpoint on general relativity becoming more and more prevalent, issues of regularity have increasingly come to the fore. In particular, while the geometric core of the theory is traditionally formulated in the smooth category, the analysis of the initial value problem, for example, requires one to consider metrics of low regularity.

Beginning in 2011 with the independent works of [FS12] and [CG12], a systematic study of Lorentzian causality theory under low regularity assumptions began and has brought to light several, sometimes surprising, facts. In a nutshell, while some features of causality theory are rather robust and topological in nature, other results are usually proved by local arguments involving geodesically convex neighbourhoods, which do exist for 𝒞1,1\mathcal{C}^{1,1}-metrics [Min15, KSS14]. Consequently for this regularity class the bulk of causality theory [CG12, Min15, KSSV14] including the singularity theorems [KSSV15, KSV15, GGKS18] remains valid. Moreover, arguments from causality theory which neither explicitly involve the exponential map nor geodesics have been found to extend to locally Lipschitz metrics, see [CG12, Thm. 1.25], [Min19, Rem. 2.5]. However, below 𝒞1,1\mathcal{C}^{1,1}, explicit counterexamples show that convex neighbourhoods may no longer exist for metrics of Hölder regularity 𝒞1,α\mathcal{C}^{1,\alpha} for any α<1\alpha<1 [HW51, SS18].

Moreover, Lorentzian causality theory has been generalized to a theory of cone structures, i.e., set-valued maps that assign a cone in the tangent space to each point on a manifold. This setting allows one to develop those aspects of the theory that merely depend on topological arguments under weak regularity assumptions. At the same time, this has led to the introduction of new methods to the field: Using weak KAM theory, existence results for smooth time functions have been derived for 𝒞0\mathcal{C}^{0}-cone structures in [FS12, Fat15], while in [BS18] dynamical systems theory has been employed to derive similar results for merely upper semi-continuous cone structures. In a landmark paper [Min19], Minguzzi has extended these studies using methods from set-valued analysis, convexity and order topology to develop large parts of causality theory for locally Lipschitz cone structures.

Returning to the metric spacetime setting, some results, such as the Avez–Seifert theorem, have been extended to 𝒞0\mathcal{C}^{0}-Lorentzian metrics [Säm16]. Moreover, a number of fundamental works on the 𝒞0\mathcal{C}^{0}-extendibility of spacetimes [Sbi18a, Sbi18b, GLS18] have appeared recently. However, already in [CG12] it was observed that two key features of causality may fail for metrics of regularity below Lipschitz:

  1. (1)

    The push up principle, i.e., (I+∘J+)∪(J+∘I+)⊆I+\left(I^{+}\circ J^{+}\right)\cup\left(J^{+}\circ I^{+}\right)\subseteq I^{+}, may cease to hold11 1 Here I+I^{+} and J+J^{+} denote the chronological and the causal relation, respectively, and e.g. I+∘J+={(p,r)∈M×M:∃q∈MI^{+}\circ J^{+}=\{(p,r)\in M\times M:\exists q\in M with (p,q)∈J+(p,q)\in J^{+} and (q,r)∈I+}(q,r)\in I^{+}\}.;

  2. (2)

    Light cones may cease to be hypersurfaces as they “bubble up” to have a nonempty interior.

Moreover, some fundamental questions raised in [CG12] remained open, especially the openness of the chronological future I+​(p)I^{+}(p) of a point pp. In this paper, we answer this question (in the negative) and clarify its relation to points (1) and (2) above. This leads to a number of natural questions concerning the relation between causal and timelike futures and pasts when defined using various classes of curves (like Lipschitz or piecewise 𝒞1\mathcal{C}^{1}). To answer these, we construct several counterexamples that exhibit a further breakdown of standard causality properties beyond those already investigated in [CG12].

Classical accounts on causality theory mainly use piecewise 𝒞1\mathcal{C}^{1}-curves. It has to be noted, however, that limit curve theorems, which form a fundamental tool in causality theory, fail to respect this regularity class. This has led Chruściel in [Chr11] to base smooth causality theory entirely on the class of locally Lipschitz curves, an approach that has been adopted in most of the subsequent studies in low regularity. In fact, Chruściel put it as follows in [Chr11, p. 14]:

“In previous treatments of causality theory [BEE96, Ger70, HE73, O’N83, Pen72, Wal84] one defines future directed timelike paths as those paths γ\gamma which are piecewise differentiable, with γ˙\dot{\gamma} timelike and future directed wherever defined; at break points one further assumes that both the left-sided and right-sided derivatives are timelike. This definition turns out to be quite inconvenient for several purposes. For instance, when studying the global causal structure of space-times one needs to take limits of timelike curves, obtaining thus — by definition — causal future directed paths. Such limits will not be piecewise differentiable most of the time, which leads one to the necessity of considering paths with poorer differentiability properties. One then faces the unhandy situation in which timelike and causal paths have completely different properties. In several theorems separate proofs have then to be given. The approach we present avoids this, leading — we believe — to a considerable simplification of the conceptual structure of the theory.”

Besides the above, a strong reason for basing causality theory entirely on locally Lipschitz curves comes from the desire to develop synthetic methods in Lorentzian geometry. In fact, following the pioneering works [Har82, AB08], recently methods from synthetic geometry and, in particular, length spaces have been implemented in the Lorentzian setting and in causality theory [KS18, GKS19]. In this framework, which generalizes low regularity Lorentzian geometry to the level of metric spaces, 𝒞1\mathcal{C}^{1}-curves are not available. Thus one needs a broad enough framework within which to address the problems highlighted by the examples given in Section 3 of the present paper.

This article is structured as follows. In Section 2 we define the basic notions of causality theory in several variants and establish some fundamental relations between them. We then introduce tools tailored to low regularity, which enable us to characterise openness of chronological futures and pasts, relate non-bubbling with push-up and clarify several aspects of pathological behaviour of continuous spacetimes. In Section 3 we provide explicit continuous spacetimes that display various pathologies. In particular, we give for the first time examples where the chronological future is not open and where the chronological future defined via smooth curves and the one defined via Lipschitz curves differ. This answers several open questions raised in [CG12]. The final section provides an overview of the interdependence of the various causality notions studied in this work.

To conclude this introduction we introduce some basic notation. Throughout this paper, MM will denote a smooth connected second countable Hausdorff manifold. Unless otherwise stated, gg will be a continuous Lorentzian metric on MM, and we will assume that (M,g)(M,g) is time-oriented (i.e., there exists a continuous timelike vector field ξ\xi, that is, g⁡(ξ,ξ)<0g(\xi,\xi)<0 everywhere). We then call (M,g)(M,g) a continuous spacetime. We shall also fix a smooth complete Riemannian metric hh on MM and denote the induced (length) metric by dhd_{h} and the induced norm by ∥.∥h\|.\|_{h}. Given Lorentzian metrics g1g_{1}, g2g_{2}, we say that g2g_{2} has strictly wider light cones than g1g_{1}, denoted by g1≺g2g_{1}\prec g_{2}, if for any tangent vector X≠0X\neq 0, g1​(X,X)⩽0g_{1}(X,X)\leqslant 0 implies that g2​(X,X)<0g_{2}(X,X)<0 (cf. [MS08, Sec. 3.8.2], [CG12, Sec. 1.2]). Thus any g1g_{1}-causal vector is timelike for g2g_{2}.

2. Curves, bubbles, and open questions

For Lorentzian metrics of regularity at least 𝒞2\mathcal{C}^{2}, chronological futures and pasts are usually defined via piecewise 𝒞1\mathcal{C}^{1} (or 𝒞∞\mathcal{C}^{\infty})-curves (e.g., [HE73, O’N83, BEE96, MS08]). Especially when working in lower regularity, several authors have employed more general classes of curves, the widest one being that of absolutely continuous curves, basically due to the fact that this is the largest class of functions for which the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus holds. This in turn is required to obtain a reasonable notion of length of curves and to control the curves via their causality. To see this let c:[0,1]→[0,1]c\colon[0,1]\rightarrow[0,1] be the Cantor function (which has bounded variation) and consider the curve γ:\gamma: [0,1]∋t↦(c⁡(t),0)[0,1]\ni t\mapsto(c(t),0) in two-dimensional Minkowski spacetime ℝ12\mathbb{R}^{2}_{1}. Then γ\gamma parametrizes the timelike curve [0,1]∋t↦(t,0)[0,1]\ni t\mapsto(t,0), but its tangent is (0,0)(0,0) almost everywhere, i.e., spacelike.

Furthermore, absolutely continuous causal curves always possess a locally Lipschitz reparametrisation (cf. Lemma 2.8 below). On the other hand, irrespective of the regularity of the metric, the limit curve theorems ([Min08]), which are of central importance in causality theory, even when applied to families of smooth causal curves typically yield curves that are merely locally Lipschitz continuous. It is therefore natural to define causal futures and pasts using such curves, and indeed it was demonstrated in [Chr11, CG12, Min15, KSSV14] for spacetimes, as well as in the significantly more general setting of cone structures in [FS12, BS18, Min19] that a fully satisfactory causality theory can be based on locally Lipschitz causal curves. As we shall see below, the situation is more involved in the case of timelike curves.

To discuss the dependence of causality theory on the underlying notions of timelike respectively causal curves, we introduce the following notations:

Definition 2.1.

We denote by

  1. (1)

    𝒜​𝒞\mathcal{AC} the set of all absolutely continuous curves from an interval into MM.

  2. (2)

    ℒ\mathcal{L} the set of all locally Lipschitz curves from an interval into MM.

  3. (3)

    𝒞pw1\mathcal{C}^{1}_{\mathrm{pw}} the set of all piecewise continuously differentiable curves from an interval into MM.

  4. (4)

    𝒞∞\mathcal{C}^{\infty} the set of all smooth curves from an interval into MM.

Here, a curve is called absolutely continuous if its components in any chart are absolutely continuous, or, equivalently, if it is absolutely continuous as a map into the metric space (M,dh)(M,d_{h}), where we recall that dhd_{h} is the metric on MM induced by the Riemannian metric hh on MM (cf. the discussion preceding Thm. 6 in [Min15]).

Clearly, we have

𝒞∞⊊𝒞pw1⊊ℒ⊊𝒜​𝒞.\mathcal{C}^{\infty}\subsetneq\mathcal{C}^{1}_{\mathrm{pw}}\subsetneq\mathcal{L}\subsetneq\mathcal{AC}. (2.1)

Henceforth, when we say that a curve γ\gamma in 𝒜​𝒞\mathcal{AC} is in fact an element of one of these smaller classes then we mean that there exists a re-parametrization of γ\gamma that lies in this class.

The definition typically employed in the smooth case (cf. the above references), but sometimes also used for continuous metrics (e.g. in [Sbi18a]), is the following.

Definition 2.2.

Let γ∈𝒞pw1\gamma\in\mathcal{C}^{1}_{\mathrm{pw}}, then γ\gamma is called

  1. timelike if g⁡(γ˙,γ˙)<0g(\dot{\gamma},\dot{\gamma})<0 everywhere.

  2. causal if g⁡(γ˙,γ˙)≤0g(\dot{\gamma},\dot{\gamma})\leq 0 and γ˙≠0\dot{\gamma}\neq 0 everywhere.

At breakpoints, the understanding is that the above conditions are satisfied for both the one-sided tangents. A causal curve γ\gamma is called future (past) directed if γ˙\dot{\gamma} belongs to the future (past) light cone everywhere (at the breakpoints this means that both one-sided tangents belong to the same light cone).

The usual definition of causal curves of regularity below piecewise 𝒞1\mathcal{C}^{1} is as follows (cf. [CG12, Def. 1.3]).

Definition 2.3.

Let γ∈𝒜​𝒞\gamma\in\mathcal{AC}, then γ\gamma is called

  1. (1)

    timelike if g⁡(γ˙,γ˙)<0g(\dot{\gamma},\dot{\gamma})<0 almost everywhere,

  2. (2)

    causal if g⁡(γ˙,γ˙)≤0g(\dot{\gamma},\dot{\gamma})\leq 0 and γ˙≠0\dot{\gamma}\neq 0 almost everywhere.

A causal curve γ\gamma is called future (past) directed if γ˙\dot{\gamma} belongs to the future (past) light cone almost everywhere.

Remark 2.4.

In [BS18], there is one further notion of timelike curve that we should mention: The authors call a Lipschitz curve timelike if its Clarke differential lies in the open chronological cone in the tangent space at each parameter value. They then show ([BS18, Lem. 2.11]) that, using this definition, the chronological futures and pasts of a point p∈Mp\in M are precisely the sets I𝒞∞±​(p)I^{\pm}_{\mathcal{C}^{\infty}}(p) (see Definition 2.5 below). Therefore, there is no need for a separate treatment of this approach.

Henceforth we will adhere to the following convention: Whenever a curve is in 𝒜​𝒞\mathcal{AC} we will use Definition 2.3, however if a curve is explicitly noted to be in 𝒞pw1\mathcal{C}^{1}_{\mathrm{pw}}, then we use Definition 2.2.

We now can define the chronological and causal future and past of a point depending on the class of curves chosen.

The following Lemma is an analogue of [Kri99, Lem. 3.2.1] (providing a distinguished local parametrization for continuous causal curves in smooth spacetimes) for continuous metrics and cylindrical neighbourhoods:

Lemma 2.8.

Let (M,g)(M,g) be a continuous spacetime, p∈Mp\in M and let (φ,U)(\varphi,U) be a cylindrical chart around pp. Let γ:[a,b]→U\gamma\colon[a,b]\rightarrow U be an absolutely continuous future directed causal curve. Then there is a reparametrisation γ~=γ∘ϕ\tilde{\gamma}=\gamma\circ\phi of γ\gamma, with ϕ:[c,d]→[a,b]\phi\colon[c,d]\rightarrow[a,b] strictly increasing and absolutely continuous, such that in the chart φ\varphi, for all t∈[c,d]t\in[c,d] one has

γ~​(t)=(t,γ→​(t)).\tilde{\gamma}(t)=(t,\vec{\gamma}(t))\,. (2.8)

0>ηC(γ˙,∂t)=−Cγ˙0,0>\eta_{C}(\dot{\gamma},\partial_{t})=-C\dot{\gamma}^{0}\,, (2.9)

almost everywhere. Thus γ˙0>0\dot{\gamma}^{0}>0 almost everywhere, and so γ0\gamma^{0} is strictly monotonically increasing. The previous result allows us to conclude that absolutely continuous causal curves always possess a reparametrisation that is Lipschitz-continuous. This fact was already noticed in [Min19, Rem. 2.3]. We include an alternative proof based on cylindrical neighbourhoods for convenience.

Lemma 2.9.

Let (M,g)(M,g) be a continuous spacetime. Then any causal curve in 𝒜​𝒞\mathcal{AC} is locally Lipschitz continuous, hence lies in ℒ\mathcal{L}. Thus, for any p∈Mp\in M, I𝒜​𝒞±​(p)=Iℒ±​(p)I^{\pm}_{\mathcal{AC}}(p)=I^{\pm}_{\mathcal{L}}(p) and J𝒜​𝒞±​(p)=Jℒ±​(p)J^{\pm}_{\mathcal{AC}}(p)=J^{\pm}_{\mathcal{L}}(p).

Proof.

Let γ:[a,b]→M\gamma\colon[a,b]\rightarrow M be an absolutely continuous future directed causal curve and let t0∈[a,b]t_{0}\in[a,b]. Set p:=γ⁡(t0)p:=\gamma(t_{0}) and let UU be a cylindrical neighbourhood of pp. Moreover, let δ>0\delta>0 such that γ⁡([t0−δ,t0+δ])⊆U\gamma([t_{0}-\delta,t_{0}+\delta])\subseteq U and let C>1C>1 with g≺ηCg\prec\eta_{C} on UU. Without loss of generality we can assume that γ​(t)=(t,γ→​(t))\gamma(t)=(t,\vec{\gamma}(t)) on UU by Lemma 2.8. Then γ\gamma is timelike for ηC\eta_{C} and hence

0>ηC​(γ˙,γ˙)=−C+‖γ→˙​(t)‖e2,0>\eta_{C}(\dot{\gamma},\dot{\gamma})=-C+\|\dot{\vec{\gamma}}(t)\|_{e}^{2}\,, (2.10)

where ∥.∥e\|.\|_{e} denotes the Euclidean norm in the chart. This implies that ‖γ˙‖e≤1+C<∞\|\dot{\gamma}\|_{e}\leq\sqrt{1+C}<\infty. Consequently, γ˙\dot{\gamma} is bounded and hence γ\gamma is Lipschitz continuous. ∎

Based on this result, for (M,g)(M,g) a continuous spacetime we shall henceforth define the chronological respectively causal future/past of a point by I±​(p):=I𝒜​𝒞±​(p)=Iℒ±​(p)I^{\pm}(p):=I^{\pm}_{\mathcal{AC}}(p)=I^{\pm}_{\mathcal{L}}(p) and J±​(p):=J𝒜​𝒞±​(p)=Jℒ±​(p)J^{\pm}(p):=J^{\pm}_{\mathcal{AC}}(p)=J^{\pm}_{\mathcal{L}}(p). This is in accordance with the conventions used in, e.g., [Chr11, CG12, FS12, KSSV14, Säm16, GGKS18, GL18, GLS18], and, for the case of J±​(p)J^{\pm}(p) also with [BS18, Min15, Min19].

For chronological (i.e., possessing no closed timelike curves) spacetimes we have the following characterization of openness of chronological futures and pasts:

Theorem 2.10.

Let (M,g)(M,g) be a continuous and chronological spacetime. Then the following are equivalent:

  • (i)

    For all p∈Mp\in M, I±​(p)I^{\pm}(p) is open.

  • (ii)

    For all p∈Mp\in M, ∂I±​(p)\partial I^{\pm}(p) is achronal.

  • (iii)

    For all p∈Mp\in M, ∂I±​(p)\partial I^{\pm}(p) is an achronal Lipschitz-hypersurface.

  • (iv)

    If FF is a future/past set with ∂F≠∅\partial F\not=\emptyset, then ∂F\partial F is an achronal Lipschitz-hypersurface.

Proof.

(iii)⇒\Rightarrow(ii) is clear.

(ii)⇒\Rightarrow(i): Suppose that I+​(p)I^{+}(p) were not open for some p∈Mp\in M. Then there exists some q∈I+​(p)∩∂I+​(p)q\in I^{+}(p)\cap\partial I^{+}(p). As MM is chronological, p∉I+​(p)p\not\in I^{+}(p). Since clearly p∈I+​(p)¯p\in\overline{I^{+}(p)}, it follows that p∈∂I+​(p)p\in\partial I^{+}(p). But then the elements pp and qq of ∂I+​(p)\partial I^{+}(p) can be connected by a timelike curve, contradicting achronality.

(i)⇒\Rightarrow(iv): Using cylindrical neighbourhoods, this follows exactly as in the smooth case (cf., e.g., [O’N83, Cor. 14.27]), cf. also [GL17, Proof of Thm. 2.6]. For a detailed proof see [Lec16, Thm. 2.3.5].

(iv)⇒\Rightarrow(iii): One only has to note that each ∂I+​(p)\partial I^{+}(p) is non-empty, which follows from MM being chronological, cf. the argument in (ii)⇒\Rightarrow(i) above. ∎

The spacetime (M,g)(M,g) is called causally plain ([CG12, Def. 1.16]) if every p∈Mp\in M possesses a cylindrical neighbourhood UU such that ∂Iˇ±​(p,U)=∂J±​(p,U)\partial\check{I}^{\pm}(p,U)=\partial J^{\pm}(p,U). Otherwise it is called bubbling22 2 We note that the phenomenon of bubbling, albeit not under this name, was first observed in [Chr91].. Note that whenever we work in a cylindrical chart, all topological notions (like closure, boundary, interior) refer to the relative topology in UU. If ∂Iˇ±​(p,U)≠∂J±​(p,U)\partial\check{I}^{\pm}(p,U)\not=\partial J^{\pm}(p,U), then the open and non-empty set ([CG12, Prop. 1.10 (vi)])

ℬ+​(p,U):=Iˇ−​(∂Iˇ+​(p,U),U)∩Iˇ+​(∂J+​(p,U),U)={(t,x)∈U:f−​(x)<t<f+​(x)}\mathcal{B}^{+}(p,U):=\check{I}^{-}(\partial\check{I}^{+}(p,U),U)\cap\check{I}^{+}(\partial J^{+}(p,U),U)=\{(t,x)\in U:f_{-}(x)<t<f_{+}(x)\}

is called the future bubble set of pp (and analogously for the past bubble set), cf. Figure 1. Refining this terminology, we additionally introduce the interior future bubble set

ℬint+​(p,U):=I+​(p,U)∖Iˇ+​(p,U),\mathcal{B}^{+}_{\mathrm{int}}(p,U):=I^{+}(p,U)\setminus\check{I}^{+}(p,U),

as well as the exterior future bubble set

ℬext+​(p,U):=J+​(p,U)∖I+​(p,U)¯,\mathcal{B}^{+}_{\mathrm{ext}}(p,U):=J^{+}(p,U)\setminus\overline{I^{+}(p,U)},

and analogously for the past.

Using Lemma 2.7 and Lemma 2.9, it follows that ℬint+​(p,U)\mathcal{B}^{+}_{\mathrm{int}}(p,U) consists of those points that can be reached from pp by a future directed Lipschitz timelike curve, but not by a future directed piecewise 𝒞1\mathcal{C}^{1} timelike curve. It remained an open problem in [CG12] whether spacetimes with non-trivial interior bubble sets actually exist. We will give examples of this phenomenon in the next section.

The exterior bubbling set is closely connected to push-up properties. To relate these to the concepts introduced above, let us first give a formal definition:

Definition 2.11.

A continuous spacetime (M,g)(M,g) is said to possess the push-up property if the following holds: Whenever γ:[a,b]→M\gamma\colon[a,b]\to M is a (absolutely continuous) future/past directed causal curve from p=γ⁡(a)p=\gamma(a) to q=γ⁡(b)q=\gamma(b) and if {t∈[a,b]:γ˙​(t)​ exists and is future/past directed timelike}\{t\in[a,b]:\dot{\gamma}(t)\text{ exists and is future/past directed timelike}\} has non-zero Lebesgue measure, then in any neighbourhood of γ⁡([a,b])\gamma([a,b]) there exists a future/past directed timelike Lipschitz curve connecting pp and qq. In particular, q∈I+​(p)q\in I^{+}(p) respectively q∈I−​(p)q\in I^{-}(p).

This property implies all the commonly used versions of push-up results. In particular, for an absolutely continuous causal curve γ:[a,b]→M\gamma\colon[a,b]\rightarrow M the set {t∈[a,b]:γ˙(t)\{t\in[a,b]:\dot{\gamma}(t) exists and is future/past directed timelike}\} has non-zero Lebesgue measure if and only if γ\gamma has positive length. A spacetime that possesses the push-up property in the sense of Definition 2.11 also satisfies what in [Chr11, Lemma 2.4.14] and [CG12, Lemma 1.22] are called push-up Lemma I (i.e., I+​(J+​(Ω))=I+​(Ω)I^{+}(J^{+}(\Omega))=I^{+}(\Omega) for any Ω⊆M\Omega\subseteq M) and push-up Lemma II, cf. [Chr11, Lemma 2.9.10] and [CG12, Lemma 1.24]. The following result shows that push-up is in fact equivalent to the non-existence of exterior bubbling:

Theorem 2.12.

Let (M,g)(M,g) be a continuous spacetime. The following are equivalent:

  • (i)

    For each p∈Mp\in M and each cylindrical chart UU centred at pp, ℬext±​(p,U)=∅\mathcal{B}^{\pm}_{\mathrm{ext}}(p,U)=\emptyset.

  • (ii)

    For each p∈Mp\in M and each cylindrical chart UU centred at pp, ∂I±​(p,U)=∂J±​(p,U)\partial I^{\pm}(p,U)=\partial J^{\pm}(p,U).

  • (iii)

    (M,g)(M,g) possesses the push-up property.

Proof.

We will use the facts and notations for cylindrical charts introduced prior to Lemma 2.7.

(i)⇒\Rightarrow(iii): By covering γ⁡([a,b])\gamma([a,b]) with cylindrical charts UU contained in the given neighbourhood of γ⁡([a,b])\gamma([a,b]) it suffices to show push-up for a curve γ:[a,b]→U\gamma\colon[a,b]\to U emanating from pp that is future-directed causal and such that the set A:={t∈[a,b]:γ˙​(t)​ exists and is timelike}A:=\{t\in[a,b]:\dot{\gamma}(t)\text{ exists and is timelike}\} has positive Lebesgue-measure λ⁡(A)\lambda(A). Moreover, by Lemma 2.9 we only need to work with Lipschitz curves. So we need to establish that q:=γ⁡(b)∈I+​(p,U)q:=\gamma(b)\in I^{+}(p,U). To begin with, suppose that q∈J+​(p,U)∘=epiS​(f−)q\in J^{+}(p,U)^{\circ}=\mathrm{epi}_{S}(f_{-}). Since I+​(p,U)I^{+}(p,U) is dense in J+​(p,U)J^{+}(p,U) by assumption and since ηC−1≺g\eta_{C^{-1}}\prec g on UU, we can find an element q′∈I+​(p,U)q^{\prime}\in I^{+}(p,U) such that qq lies in the ηC−1\eta_{C^{-1}}-future of q′q^{\prime}, and thereby in I+​(p,U)I^{+}(p,U) itself. Note that this argument in fact shows that J+​(p,U)∘⊆I+​(p,U)J^{+}(p,U)^{\circ}\subseteq I^{+}(p,U). We are therefore left with the case q∈∂J+​(p,U)q\in\partial J^{+}(p,U). Suppose, then, that such a qq were not contained in I+​(p,U)I^{+}(p,U).

We claim that there exists a non-trivial interval [c,d]⊆(a,b)[c,d]\subseteq(a,b) such that γ⁡([c,d])⊆I+​(p,U)\gamma([c,d])\subseteq I^{+}(p,U) and that s¯∈A\bar{s}\in A for some s¯∈(c,d)\bar{s}\in(c,d). To see this, we adapt an argument from the proof of [CG12, Prop. 1.21]. As was shown there, if t∈At\in A and γ⁡(t)∈∂J+​(p,U)\gamma(t)\in\partial J^{+}(p,U) then there exists some ε>0\varepsilon>0 such that γ⁡((,,,))\gamma((t,t+\varepsilon)) lies in J+​(p,U)∘J^{+}(p,U)^{\circ} and thereby in I+​(p,U)I^{+}(p,U) by the above. Arguing analogously to the past, it follows that ε\varepsilon can be chosen so small that also γ⁡((,,,))\gamma((t-\varepsilon,t)) is disjoint from ∂J+​(p,U)\partial J^{+}(p,U) (in fact, lies in hypS​(f−)\mathrm{hyp}_{S}(f_{-})). To prove our claim, it suffices to show that there exists some s∈As\in A with γ⁡(s)∉∂J+​(p,U)\gamma(s)\not\in\partial J^{+}(p,U) (hence γ⁡(s)∈epiS​(f−)\gamma(s)\in\mathrm{epi}_{S}(f_{-})), as then also a non-trivial interval around ss is mapped by γ\gamma to epiS​(f−)\mathrm{epi}_{S}(f_{-}). So it only remains to exclude the possibility that γ⁡(s)∈∂J+​(p,U)\gamma(s)\in\partial J^{+}(p,U) for each s∈As\in A. To do this, we note that since λ⁡(A)>0\lambda(A)>0, AA must contain accumulation points of AA (otherwise AA would consist of isolated points and thereby be countable). However, if s∈As\in A is such an accumulation point and sks_{k} is a sequence in AA converging to ss, then choosing ε\varepsilon as above for ss we obtain that sk∈(s−ε,s+ε)∖{s}s_{k}\in(s-\varepsilon,s+\varepsilon)\setminus\{s\} for kk large, contradicting the assumption that γ⁡(A)⊆∂J+​(p,U)\gamma(A)\subseteq\partial J^{+}(p,U).

Now let fq−f_{q}^{-} be the graphing function of ∂J−​(q,U)\partial J^{-}(q,U).33 3 It follows from the proof of [CG12, Prop. 1.10] that the cylindrical neighbourhood UU of pp can be chosen ‘locally uniformly’ in the sense that each q∈Uq\in U possesses a cylindrical chart with domain UU. Then no point rr in γ⁡([c,d])\gamma([c,d]) can lie strictly below the graph of fq−f_{q}^{-} since otherwise r∈I−​(q,U)∩I+​(p,U)r\in I^{-}(q,U)\cap I^{+}(p,U), and a fortiori q∈I+​(p,U)q\in I^{+}(p,U), contrary to our assumption. Hence γ|[c,d]\gamma|_{[c,d]} must lie on the graph of fq−f_{q}^{-}. But then the same argument as above, using fq−f_{q}^{-} and working in the past direction leads to a contradiction since at γ⁡(s¯)\gamma(\bar{s}) the curve must enter I−​(q,U)I^{-}(q,U). Summing up, we conclude that q∈I+​(p,U)q\in I^{+}(p,U), as claimed.

(iii)⇒\Rightarrow(ii): Since ∂t\partial_{t} is future-directed timelike, (iii) implies that J+​(p,U)∘=epiS​(f−)⊆I+​(p,U)J^{+}(p,U)^{\circ}=\mathrm{epi}_{S}(f_{-})\subseteq I^{+}(p,U), so ∂I+​(p,U)=I+​(p,U)¯∖I+​(p,U)∘⊆∂J+​(p,U)\partial I^{+}(p,U)=\overline{I^{+}(p,U)}\setminus I^{+}(p,U)^{\circ}\subseteq\partial J^{+}(p,U). Conversely, considering a vertical line through any point qq in ∂J+​(p,U)\partial J^{+}(p,U) and using push-up again, it follows that in any neighbourhood of qq there lie points from I+​(p,U)∘I^{+}(p,U)^{\circ} as well as points from the complement of I+​(p,U)¯\overline{I^{+}(p,U)}, so q∈∂I+​(p,U)q\in\partial I^{+}(p,U).

(ii)⇒\Rightarrow(i): Since J+​(p,U)=epi⁡(f−)=epiS​(f−)¯=J+​(p,U)∘¯J^{+}(p,U)=\mathrm{epi}(f_{-})=\overline{\mathrm{epi}_{S}(f_{-})}=\overline{J^{+}(p,U)^{\circ}}, it suffices to show that J+​(p,U)∘⊆I+​(p,U)J^{+}(p,U)^{\circ}\subseteq I^{+}(p,U). Suppose, to the contrary, that there exists some q∈J+​(p,U)∘∖I+​(p,U)q\in J^{+}(p,U)^{\circ}\setminus I^{+}(p,U). We can then connect qq via a continuous path α\alpha that runs entirely in J+​(p,U)∘J^{+}(p,U)^{\circ} with a point in I+​(p,U)I^{+}(p,U) (e.g., with any point on the positive tt-axis). But then α\alpha has to intersect ∂I+​(p,U)\partial I^{+}(p,U), producing a point in ∂I+​(p,U)∖∂J+​(p,U)\partial I^{+}(p,U)\setminus\partial J^{+}(p,U), a contradiction. ∎

Remark 2.13.

We note that the equivalence between the push-up property and the absence of causal bubbles was first observed, even in the more general setting of closed cone structures (with chronological futures/pasts defined via piecewise 𝒞1\mathcal{C}^{1}-curves) by E. Minguzzi in [Min19, Thm. 2.8].

Concerning the relationship between the various bubble sets we have:

Lemma 2.14.

Let (M,g)(M,g) be a continuous spacetime and let UU be a cylindrical neighbourhood of p∈Mp\in M. Then

{f−(x)<t<f+(x)}=ℬ+(p,U)⊆ℬint+​(p,U)¯∪ℬext+(p,U)⊆{f−(x)⩽t⩽f+(x)},\{f_{-}(x)<t<f_{+}(x)\}=\mathcal{B}^{+}(p,U)\subseteq\overline{\mathcal{B}^{+}_{\mathrm{int}}(p,U)}\cup\mathcal{B}^{+}_{\mathrm{ext}}(p,U)\subseteq\{f_{-}(x)\leqslant t\leqslant f_{+}(x)\}, (2.11)

and analogously for the past-directed case.

Proof.

By [CG12, Prop. 1.10] and [CG12, Prop. 1.21], the bubble set ℬ+​(p,U)\mathcal{B}^{+}(p,U) is the intersection of epiS​(f−)\mathrm{epi}_{S}(f_{-}) and the strict hypograph hypS​(f+)\mathrm{hyp}_{S}(f_{+}) of the graphing function f+f_{+} of ∂Iˇ+​(p,U)\partial\check{I}^{+}(p,U). From this, the second inclusion follows immediately. To see the first one, note that by the properties of cylindrical neighbourhoods detailed before Lemma 2.7, any p∈ℬ+​(p,U)p\in\mathcal{B}^{+}(p,U) is contained in J+​(p,U)∖Iˇ+​(p,U)¯J^{+}(p,U)\setminus\overline{\check{I}^{+}(p,U)}. Now suppose, in addition, that p∉ℬint+​(p,U)¯⊇I+​(p,U)¯∖Iˇ+​(p,U)¯p\not\in\overline{\mathcal{B}^{+}_{\mathrm{int}}(p,U)}\supseteq\overline{I^{+}(p,U)}\setminus\overline{\check{I}^{+}(p,U)}. Then p∈J+​(p,U)∖I+​(p,U)¯=ℬext+​(p,U)p\in J^{+}(p,U)\setminus\overline{I^{+}(p,U)}=\mathcal{B}^{+}_{\mathrm{ext}}(p,U). ∎

From Lemma 2.7 and Lemma 2.9 we obtain:

Theorem 2.15.

Let (M,g)(M,g) be a continuous spacetime. The following are equivalent:

  • (i)

    For any p∈Mp\in M,

    I𝒞∞±​(p)=I𝒞pw1±​(p)=Iℒ±​(p)=I𝒜​𝒞±​(p).I^{\pm}_{\mathcal{C}^{\infty}}(p)=I^{\pm}_{\mathcal{C}^{1}_{\mathrm{pw}}}(p)=I^{\pm}_{\mathcal{L}}(p)=I^{\pm}_{\mathcal{AC}}(p).
  • (ii)

    There is no internal bubbling, i.e., ℬint±​(p,U)=∅\mathcal{B}^{\pm}_{\mathrm{int}}(p,U)=\emptyset for every p∈Mp\in M and every cylindrical neighbourhood UU of pp.

  • (iii)

    I±​(p)=Iˇ±​(p)I^{\pm}(p)=\check{I}^{\pm}(p) for every p∈Mp\in M.

Corollary 2.16.

Let (M,g)(M,g) be a continuous spacetime. The following are equivalent:

  1. (i)

    (M,g)(M,g) is causally plain.

  2. (ii)

    There is neither internal nor external bubbling, i.e. ℬint±​(p,U)=ℬext±​(p,U)=∅\mathcal{B}^{\pm}_{\mathrm{int}}(p,U)=\mathcal{B}^{\pm}_{\mathrm{ext}}(p,U)=\emptyset, for all p∈Mp\in M.

Proof.

Let (M,g)(M,g) be causally plain. By [CG12, Prop. 1.21], we have Iˇ±​(p)=I±​(p)\check{I}^{\pm}(p)=I^{\pm}(p) for all p∈Mp\in M, so there is no interior bubbling. By [CG12, Lemma 1.22], (M,g)(M,g) has the push-up property, so, by Theorem 2.12, we have ℬext±​(p,U)=∅\mathcal{B}^{\pm}_{\mathrm{ext}}(p,U)=\emptyset.

The other direction follows directly from Lemma 2.14. ∎

Any spacetime with a Lipschitz continuous metric is causally plain by [CG12, Cor. 1.17] and so, by Corollary 2.16, such a spacetime has neither internal nor external bubbling. Moreover, by Theorem 2.15, for spacetimes without internal bubbling, it does not matter which type of curves is used in the definition of chronological futures and pasts.

After these preparations we can now formulate the questions that will be addressed in the remainder of this paper. Let (M,g)(M,g) be a continuous spacetime. The following two questions have already been posed in [CG12]:

  1. (Q1)

    Is I±​(p)I^{\pm}(p) open for each pp?

  2. (Q2)

    Is I±​(p)=Iˇ±​(p)I^{\pm}(p)=\check{I}^{\pm}(p) for each pp?

According to Theorem 2.15, (Q2) is equivalent to the question

  • (Q2′)

    Is it true that, for all p∈Mp\in M, I𝒞∞±​(p)=I𝒞pw1±​(p)=Iℒ±​(p)=I𝒜​𝒞±​(p)I^{\pm}_{\mathcal{C}^{\infty}}(p)=I^{\pm}_{\mathcal{C}^{1}_{\mathrm{pw}}}(p)=I^{\pm}_{\mathcal{L}}(p)=I^{\pm}_{\mathcal{AC}}(p)?

Obviously, for spacetimes such that (Q2) can be answered affirmatively, the same is true for (Q1). It is natural to ask for the converse of this implication:

  1. (3)

    Does an affirmative answer to (Q1) for a given spacetime imply the same for (Q2)?

Heuristically speaking, to call a set a bubble, one would expect it to have a non-empty interior. A natural question that therefore arises is the following.

  1. (4)

    Is Iˇ+​(p)\check{I}^{+}(p) dense in I+​(p)I^{+}(p), i.e., is I±​(p)⊆Iˇ±​(p)¯I^{\pm}(p)\subseteq\overline{\check{I}^{\pm}(p)}, for all p∈Mp\in M?

Finally, we address the relation between bubbling and interior bubbling: As noted above, non-bubbling, i.e., causally plain, spacetimes cannot exhibit interior bubbling. On the other hand, in the only currently known examples of bubbling metrics ([CG12, Ex. 1.11]) there is no interior bubbling, so all bubble sets are exterior (i.e., lie outside of I+​(p,U)¯\overline{I^{+}(p,U)}). Another natural question is therefore:

  1. (5)

    Given a non-causally plain spacetime, are all bubble sets of the same type (interior or exterior)?

In the following section, we provide examples that answer all of these questions in the negative.

3. Counterexamples

In this section, we present examples of Lorentzian metrics which show that the answers to the questions (Q1)–(5) are negative. The metrics are all defined on a two-dimensional domain Ω⊆ℝ2\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{2} with coordinates (t,x)(t,x), and are taken to be of the form

𝐠:=2​[−sin⁡2​θ​(t,x)​d​t2−2​cos⁡2​θ​(t,x)​d​x​d​t+sin⁡2​θ​(t,x)​d​x2]\mathbf{g}:=2\left[-\sin 2\theta(t,x)\,dt^{2}-2\cos 2\theta(t,x)\,dx\,dt+\sin 2\theta(t,x)\,dx^{2}\right] (3.1)

for an appropriately chosen function θ⁡(t,x)\theta(t,x). Note that this metric has the property that the vectors

v1:=cosθ(t,x)∂x+sinθ(t,x)∂t,v2:=cosθ(t,x)∂t−sinθ(t,x)∂xv_{1}:=\cos\theta(t,x)\,\partial_{x}+\sin\theta(t,x)\,\partial_{t},\qquad v_{2}:=\cos\theta(t,x)\,\partial_{t}-\sin\theta(t,x)\,\partial_{x}

are null, and 𝐠⁡(v1,v2)=−2\mathbf{g}(v_{1},v_{2})=-2.

Example 3.1.

Let Ω:=ℝ2\Omega:=\mathbb{R}^{2} and 0<α<10<\alpha<1. We define the function

θ⁡(t,x)≡θ⁡(x):={0,x<−1,arccos⁡|x|α,−1⩽x⩽0,π2,x>0.\theta(t,x)\equiv\theta(x):=\begin{cases}0,&x<-1,\\ \arccos|x|^{\alpha},&-1\leqslant x\leqslant 0,\\ \frac{\pi}{2},&x>0.\end{cases}

With this function θ\theta, the metric (3.1) is α\alpha-Hölder continuous, but not Lipschitz. It is smooth away from x=0x=0 and x=−1x=-1. If we wish to confine the non-smooth behaviour of the metric to the tt-axis alone, we may restrict to the region x∈(−1,∞)x\in(-1,\infty). Alternatively, we may simply smooth out the metric near the set x=−1x=-1.

The light cones of this metric are illustrated in Figure 2.

If we consider a null generator parametrised by its xx-value leaving a point pp with t⁡(p)=t0t(p)=t_{0}, x⁡(p)=−1x(p)=-1 tangent to the xx-axis, then its tangent vector will be proportional to v1v_{1} and, as such, t⁡(x)t(x) will satisfy the ordinary differential equation

d​td​x=tan⁡θ⁡(t,x)=(1−|x|2​α)1/2|x|α,\frac{dt}{dx}=\tan\theta(t,x)=\frac{\left(1-|x|^{2\alpha}\right)^{1/2}}{|x|^{\alpha}},

for x∈(−1,0]x\in(-1,0] with t⁡(−1)=t0t(-1)=t_{0}. Therefore, the generator will reach the tt-axis, i.e. x=0x=0, at time

t1:=t0+∫−10(1−|x|2​α)1/2|x|α​𝑑x<∞.t_{1}:=t_{0}+\int_{-1}^{0}\frac{\left(1-|x|^{2\alpha}\right)^{1/2}}{|x|^{\alpha}}\,dx<\infty.

Note that this argument crucially relies on the fact that α<1\alpha<1. If gg were Lipschitz (α=1\alpha=1), for example, the above curve does not reach the tt-axis in finite time. This is consistent with the fact that Lipschitz metrics are causally plain (cf. Corollary 2.16).

The generator constructed above reaches the tt-axis at a finite value t1>t0t_{1}>t_{0}, and can then be continued vertically up the tt-axis as a null generator of ∂J+​(p)\partial J^{+}(p). Indeed, we note that any absolutely continuous, future-directed, causal curve from a point on the tt-axis cannot enter the region x>0x>0. In particular, let α:[0,∞)→ℝ2\alpha\colon[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}^{2} be an absolutely continuous, future-directed, causal curve with (x∘α)​(0)=0\left(x\circ\alpha\right)(0)=0, and assume that there exists s0>0s_{0}>0 such that (x∘α)​(s0)>0\left(x\circ\alpha\right)(s_{0})>0. Then, there exists a subset B⊆[0,∞)B\subseteq[0,\infty) with positive Lebesgue measure such that for all s∈Bs\in B, dd​s​(x∘α)​(s)\frac{d}{ds}\left(x\circ\alpha\right)(s) exists and is strictly positive. This contradicts the assumption that the curve α\alpha is future-directed causal, i.e. that α˙​(s)\dot{\alpha}(s) is future-directed causal almost everywhere.

The preceding observation implies that the set J+​(p)J^{+}(p) consists of the light blue region in Figure 2, along with the vertical null generator from pp and the right-moving null generator from pp. (In particular, the subset of the tt-axis with t⩾t1t\geqslant t_{1} is part of the boundary of J+​(p)J^{+}(p).)

We now note, however, that any point (t,0)(t,0) in the null cone of pp with t>t1t>t_{1} can also be reached by a curve from pp that is 𝒞1\mathcal{C}^{1} and timelike at all points except the intersection of the curve with the tt-axis. In particular, let q=(t¯,0)q=(\overline{t},0) with t¯>t1\overline{t}>t_{1}. Then q∈∂I+​(p)q\in\partial I^{+}(p). As such, the curve γ\gamma is timelike for small s<0s<0 and null only at s=0s=0. It follows that, for small s0<0s_{0}<0, the point γ⁡(s0)\gamma(s_{0}) lies in I+​(p)I^{+}(p). Since the metric gg is smooth for x<0x<0, there exists a 𝒞1\mathcal{C}^{1} timelike curve from pp to γ⁡(s0)\gamma(s_{0}). We may assume, without loss of generality, that the tangent vector of this curve coincides with that of the curve γ\gamma at the point γ⁡(s0)\gamma(s_{0}). Concatenating this curve with the restriction of γ\gamma to (s0,0](s_{0},0] gives a curve c:[−1,0]→ℝ2c\colon[-1,0]\to\mathbb{R}^{2} with c⁡(−1)=pc(-1)=p, c⁡(0)=q∈∂J+​(p)c(0)=q\in\partial J^{+}(p), that is 𝒞1\mathcal{C}^{1} with timelike tangent vector on the open interval (−1,0)(-1,0) and whose tangent vector at qq is null.

This example has the following properties:

  • •

    The chronological future of any point with x<0x<0 is not an open subset of ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}. In particular, I+​(p)I^{+}(p) consists of the light blue region in Figure 2, including the subset of the tt-axis with t>t1t>t_{1}. This answers (Q1) in the negative.

  • •

    Iˇ+​(p)\check{I}^{+}(p) consists of the light blue region in Figure 2, excluding the subset of the tt-axis with t>t1t>t_{1}. As such, Iˇ+​(p)≠I+​(p)\check{I}^{+}(p)\neq I^{+}(p). This answers (Q2) in the negative.

  • •

    The exceptional curve cc constructed in the example may be taken to be smooth, with only one point at which it is null. It may be extended in a timelike fashion to give a curve that is smooth except at one point of non-differentiability, and timelike everywhere where its derivative is defined (at which point, the tangent vector from the past direction is null and the tangent vector to the future is timelike). As such, the curve is not timelike in the sense of Definition 2.2, but it is timelike in the sense of Definition 2.3.

  • •

    Since Iˇ+​(p)\check{I}^{+}(p) is not equal to I+​(p)I^{+}(p), it follows from Theorem 2.15 and Corollary 2.16 that the spacetime cannot be causally plain, so there must exist a point r∈Mr\in M with ℬ±​(r,U)≠∅\mathcal{B}^{\pm}(r,U)\neq\emptyset, for some cylindrical neighbourhood UU of rr. Indeed, while the bubble set of pp is empty, every point on the tt-axis has a non-empty past bubble set. This behaviour will be even more pronounced in the following example.

Example 3.2.

Let (t,x)∈Ω=ℝ2(t,x)\in\Omega=\mathbb{R}^{2}, and 0<α<10<\alpha<1. We take the metric to be of the form (3.1), but with

θ⁡(t,x)≡θ⁡(x):={0,x<−1,arccos⁡|x|α,−1⩽x⩽1,0,x>1.\theta(t,x)\equiv\theta(x):=\begin{cases}0,&x<-1,\\ \arccos|x|^{\alpha},&-1\leqslant x\leqslant 1,\\ 0,&x>1.\end{cases}

As in Example 3.1, the metric (3.1) is α\alpha-Hölder but not Lipschitz, and smooth away from x=0,±1x=0,\pm 1.

The light cone structure for this metric is illustrated in Figure 3.

For the point pp in the figure, the light blue set is the set Iˇ+​(p)\check{I}^{+}(p), while the union of the light blue and dark blue sets (including all points on the tt-axis above the point pp) is the set I+​(p)I^{+}(p). As such, non-trivial internal bubbling occurs for this metric. In particular,

  • •

    The set I+​(q)I^{+}(q) is open for all points q∈ℝ2q\in\mathbb{R}^{2}. However, for the particular point pp in Figure 3, we have that I±​(p)≠Iˇ±​(p)I^{\pm}(p)\neq\check{I}^{\pm}(p). This shows that the answer to (3) is negative.

  • •

    For the point pp in Figure 3, the set Iˇ+​(p)\check{I}^{+}(p) is contained in the region x<0x<0, while I+​(p)I^{+}(p) contains a subset of the region x>0x>0 with non-empty interior. It follows that Iˇ+​(p)\check{I}^{+}(p) is not a dense subset of I+​(p)I^{+}(p) in this spacetime. Therefore, this example answers (4) in the negative.

Example 3.3.

In [CG12], the 𝒞0,λ\mathcal{C}^{0,\lambda} metric

𝐠=−(d​u+(1−|u|λ)​d​x)2+d​x2\mathbf{g}=-\left(du+\left(1-|u|^{\lambda}\right)dx\right)^{2}+dx^{2} (3.2)

for (u,x)∈ℝ2(u,x)\in\mathbb{R}^{2} with 0<λ<10<\lambda<1 was considered, which exhibits external bubbling. In our next example, we define a different metric where the external bubbling effect is localised. We then glue this metric into Example 3.2 above to construct a metric where there exists a point p∈Mp\in M such that Iˇ+​(p)⊊I+​(p)\check{I}^{+}(p)\subsetneq I^{+}(p) and I+​(p)¯⊊J+​(p)\overline{I^{+}(p)}\subsetneq J^{+}(p) at the same time.

Let x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R}, t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R}, and 0<α,λ<10<\alpha,\lambda<1. Let θ0:=arccos⁡(12)α\theta_{0}:=\arccos\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{\alpha}, and fix ρ∈(0,1)\rho\in\left(0,1\right) such that arctan⁡ρλ<θ0\arctan\rho^{\lambda}<\theta_{0}. We define the regions

A:={(t,x)∈[−ρ,ρ]×[−56,−23]},B:={(t,x)∈[−1,1]×[−1,−12]}.A:=\left\{(t,x)\in\left[-\rho,\rho\right]\times\left[-\frac{5}{6},-\frac{2}{3}\right]\right\},\qquad B:=\left\{(t,x)\in\left[-1,1\right]\times\left[-1,-\frac{1}{2}\right]\right\}.

We consider the Lorentzian metric (3.1) where the function θ⁡(t,x)\theta(t,x) is defined as follows:

  • ∙\bullet

    θ⁡(t,x):={0,x<−1,arccos⁡|x|α,−1⩽x⩽1,0,x>1;\theta(t,x):=\begin{cases}0,&x<-1,\\ \arccos|x|^{\alpha},&-1\leqslant x\leqslant 1,\\ 0,&x>1;\end{cases}
  • ∙\bullet

    For (t,x)∈A(t,x)\in A, let

    θ⁡(t,x):=arctan⁡|t|λ;\theta(t,x):=\arctan|t|^{\lambda};
  • ∙\bullet

    We choose the function θ\theta on the set B∖AB\setminus A in such a way that

    1. (i).

      θ\theta is continuous on M≡ℝ2M\equiv\mathbb{R}^{2};

    2. (ii).

      For each fixed t∈[−1,1]t\in[-1,1] the angle θ⁡(t,x)\theta(t,x) is a non-decreasing function of x∈[−1,0]x\in[-1,0], i.e., for each fixed t∈[−ρ,ρ]t\in\left[-\rho,\rho\right], the function x↦θ⁡(t,x)x\mapsto\theta(t,x) is non-decreasing;

      θ⁡(t,−1)=0,θ⁡(t,−12)=arccos⁡(12)α,∀t∈[−1,1],\theta\left(t,-1\right)=0,\qquad\theta\left(t,-\frac{1}{2}\right)=\arccos\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{\alpha},\qquad\forall t\in[-1,1],

Remark 3.4.

The function θ⁡(t,x)\theta(t,x) may be chosen to be smooth away from the tt-axis and the points of the set AA that lie on the xx-axis. Globally, we then have that θ\theta has Hölder regularity 𝒞0,β\mathcal{C}^{0,\beta}, with β:=min⁡(α,λ)\beta:=\min(\alpha,\lambda).

The right-moving null generators leaving a point t=0t=0, x∈(−56,−23)x\in(-\frac{5}{6},-\frac{2}{3}) in the region AA satisfy

d​td​x=|t|λ.\frac{dt}{dx}=|t|^{\lambda}.

The non-uniqueness of the solutions to this equation leads to the same external bubbling effect demonstrated by the metric (3.2) (cf. [CG12]). In our case, however, this non-uniqueness effect is localised within the region AA.

Let q=(0,x0)q=(0,x_{0}) be a point in the interior of the set AA. We denote by γ0\gamma_{0} the right-moving null generator from qq that immediately leaves the xx-axis at qq, i.e. t​(γ0​(s))>0t(\gamma_{0}(s))>0 for all s>0s>0. However, right-moving null generators from qq can travel along the xx-axis for a finite time, and then leave the xx-axis. We denote by γ1\gamma_{1} the right-moving null generator from qq that leaves the xx-axis at the largest value of xx, i.e. γ1\gamma_{1} leaves the xx-axis at the point (0,x1)(0,x_{1}) where x0<−23⩽x1<−12x_{0}<-\frac{2}{3}\leqslant x_{1}<-\frac{1}{2}. The null generators γ0\gamma_{0}, γ1\gamma_{1} later intersect the tt-axis at the points (t0,0)(t_{0},0), (t1,0)(t_{1},0), respectively, where t1<t0t_{1}<t_{0}. The set J+​(q)∖I+​(q)¯J^{+}(q)\setminus\overline{I^{+}(q)} contains the area between γ0\gamma_{0} and γ1\gamma_{1} up to the tt-axis, and hence has non-empty interior. As in Example 3.2, for any t¯>t0\overline{t}>t_{0}, the point (t¯,0)∈I+​(q)(\overline{t},0)\in I^{+}(q) and I+​(t¯,0)I^{+}(\overline{t},0) contains a subset of the set x>0x>0 with non-empty interior. Since Iˇ+​(q)\check{I}^{+}(q) is contained in the set x<0x<0, it follows that I+​(q)∖Iˇ+​(q)I^{+}(q)\setminus\check{I}^{+}(q) has non-empty interior as well.

This example therefore answers (5) in the negative, and indeed shows that there exist points qq in the spacetime such that ℬext+​(q,U)\mathcal{B}^{+}_{\mathrm{ext}}(q,U) is non-empty for some cylindrical neighbourhood UU of qq, and Iˇ+​(q)≠I+​(q)\check{I}^{+}(q)\neq I^{+}(q).

Remark 3.5.

In all of the above examples, the exceptional curves can, in fact, be chosen to be 𝒞1\mathcal{C}^{1} with non-timelike tangent vector at only one point. Heuristically, one might expect that the seemingly innocuous change of allowing 𝒞1\mathcal{C}^{1} curves that have timelike tangent vector except at a finite number of points at which the tangent vector may be null should not affect chronological pasts and futures. However, our examples show that in fact all of the pathologies exhibited above would persist if this definition were adopted.

4. Conclusions

The following diagram collects the (non-)implications between the causal regularity properties we have studied in the previous sections. Let (M,g)(M,g) be a continuous spacetime and recall that I±​(p):=I𝒜​𝒞±​(p)=Iℒ±​(p)I^{\pm}(p):=I^{\pm}_{\mathcal{AC}}(p)=I^{\pm}_{\mathcal{L}}(p). Then:

Here, \raisebox{0.4pt}{\tiny$1$}⃝ was shown in [CG12, Cor. 1.17]. Irreversibility of this arrow can be seen by considering a metric that is conformally equivalent to the Minkowski metric via a non-Lipschitz factor. Of more interest is the fact that warped products with one-dimensional base (i.e., metrics of the form −d​t2+f2​h-dt^{2}+f^{2}h with hh any Riemannian metric and f:(a,b)→(0,∞)f:(a,b)\to(0,\infty) continuous) are causally plain for continuous, not necessarily Lipschitz, warping functions ff, cf. [AGKS19]. Equivalence \raisebox{0.4pt}{\tiny$2$}⃝ is Corollary 2.16. Irreversibility in \raisebox{0.4pt}{\tiny$3$}⃝, \raisebox{0.4pt}{\tiny$4$}⃝ and \raisebox{0.4pt}{\tiny$8$}⃝, as well as the claims in \raisebox{0.4pt}{\tiny$9$}⃝ follow from [CG12, Ex. 1.12] and Example 3.2, respectively. Equivalence \raisebox{0.4pt}{\tiny$5$}⃝ holds by Theorem 2.15, while \raisebox{0.4pt}{\tiny$6$}⃝ is a consequence of Theorem 2.12. The claims in \raisebox{0.4pt}{\tiny$7$}⃝ follow from [CG12, Ex. 1.12] and Example 3.1. Finally, Example 3.2 entails irreversibility of \raisebox{0.4pt}{\tiny$8$}⃝.

The watershed in this chain of implications is the case of causally plain spacetimes. Indeed, for such metrics all versions of chronological futures and pasts coincide. Moreover, there are no bubble sets, chronological futures and pasts are open and the standard push-up properties hold. Indeed, it was demonstrated in [KS18, Sec. 5.1] that strongly causal and causally plain spacetimes form strongly localisable Lorentzian length spaces, implying that their causality theory is optimal in the sense of synthetic low regularity Lorentzian geometry.

On the other hand, the examples in Section 3 demonstrate that continuous but non-Lipschitz spacetimes display a number of unexpected new causal phenomena that are entirely absent from the causally plain setting. The most drastic of these is the occurrence of non-open chronological futures/pasts. It is no exaggeration to state that openness of I±​(p)I^{\pm}(p) is ubiquitous throughout standard causality theory. For example, Theorem 2.10 (iv) is a property that features prominently in proofs of the singularity theorems of General Relativity: for the most general version of the causal part of these theorems we refer to [Min19, Sec. 2.15] (cf., in particular, the proof of Penrose’s singularity theorem [Min19, Thm. 65] that relies on this property in the form of [Min19, Thm. 20]). That this condition is (for chronological spacetimes) in fact equivalent to openness of chronological futures/pasts (Theorem 2.10 (i)) is a strong indication that it is preferable to adopt a different definition for these sets in regularities below Lipschitz. Indeed, the arguments put forward in this paper suggest that the optimal strategy for obtaining a satisfactory causality theory is the following:

  • •

    In order to derive the maximal benefit from limit curve theorems, set J±​(p):=J𝒜​𝒞±​(p)=Jℒ±​(p)J^{\pm}(p):=J^{\pm}_{\mathcal{AC}}(p)=J^{\pm}_{\mathcal{L}}(p) (cf. Lemma 2.9).

  • •

    To guarantee openness of chronological futures and pasts and to avoid interior bubbling, set I±​(p):=I𝒞pw1±​(p)I^{\pm}(p):=I^{\pm}_{\mathcal{C}^{1}_{\mathrm{pw}}}(p). Then in fact I±​(p)=Iˇ±​(p)=I𝒞∞±​(p)I^{\pm}(p)=\check{I}^{\pm}(p)=I^{\pm}_{\mathcal{C}^{\infty}}(p) by Lemma 2.7.

The first point here is valid across all regularities of the metric. For the second one, we have seen in Theorem 2.15 that for spacetimes without internal bubbling (in particular: for Lipschitz spacetimes) the choice of class of curves makes no difference, while the examples in Section 3 clearly underline the advantage of adhering to this convention for non-Lipschitz metrics.

While this strategy returns us to the “unhandy situation in which timelike and causal paths have completely different properties” [Chr11, p. 14], it appears to us to be the most fitting approach. Moreover, note that, in fact, several fundamental works on low regularity Lorentzian geometry have adopted these conventions, in particular [Min15, Min19, BS18] and, in the timelike case, [GL17, Sbi18a]. On the other hand, in synthetic approaches to low regularity Lorentzian geometry (such as [KS18, GKS19]), where this strategy is not an option (due to the absence of a differentiable structure), phenomena such as the ones laid out in Section 3 have to be taken into consideration.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:
